title: What the homepage has to prove for a nonprofit
metaTitle: What a nonprofit homepage has to prove
excerpt: Show the program in a real place, and offer a way to give, join, or read it. A sad photo with only a donate button does not prove the work is real.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table, for a piece on explaining a program in one scene.
caption: A working meeting, with the materials in view. A homepage should show the work this plainly. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a nonprofit homepage lead with?
faqs.answer: The program, in a place and on a schedule a stranger can picture. Who it is for, and a way to give, join, or read. A slogan about empowering communities can sit later, if it still earns a place after the scene is clear.

faqs.question: Does the homepage always need a donate button?
faqs.answer: Giving should be available when giving is real. It does not have to be the only verb, or the primary one, if enrollment or reading is the honest door this season. A person seeking the service should not have to climb a gala appeal to find the hours.

faqs.question: Which numbers belong on the homepage?
faqs.answer: Numbers you can point to in a report and define in a sentence. People served, nights open, or a cost you can explain. Lives touched, with no method, should stay off the page. One proof with a constraint and a decision is stronger than a billboard figure.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A nonprofit homepage has to prove the work is real, to a donor or a participant who is deciding whether to stay. Show the work in the world. Offer a way to give, join, or read the program. A sad photograph and a donate button, with nothing about what the program does, fails that person in the first glance.

Write the page in that order. The work, in a place a stranger can picture. Then who it is for. Then the way in. The organization's feelings about its mission can support those three. They cannot replace them.

## The work, in a real place

Name the program the way a participant or a donor would recognize it. A legal clinic on weeknights. A food program at two schools. A trail crew on a specific range. The noun is the program, the place, and the person served. A headline that says empowering communities to thrive could describe a thousand organizations, including ones this visitor will not trust.

Show that program happening. A room, a route, a counter, a class, with enough context to see what is being done. Faces only with consent, and never as a shortcut for pity. The frame should answer "what do they do on a normal week?" If you cannot answer with a picture yet, answer with three concrete sentences and a quieter image you have rights to. Emptiness is better than a borrowed crisis.

Say who it is for, and who it is not for, in a sentence each. Adults leaving incarceration in one county. Families at these two campuses. Not a general appeal to anyone with a pulse. Boundaries help the right person recognize themselves, and they help a donor see that the organization knows its own edge. A homepage that claims everyone is a homepage that has not chosen.

Place and time make the work believable. Which days, which neighborhood, what a person receives or does when they show up. You can hold the full detail for the program page. The homepage still needs one scene. "Tuesday intake, 4 to 7, at the west side clinic" does more than a paragraph about hope.

## A way to give, a way to join, a way to read

The next step is not always a donation, and the page should not pretend it is. Some visitors are there to enroll, volunteer, or refer someone. Some are there to read the program before they give. Offer the paths that are real, and make one of them primary for the season. If enrollment is open, enrollment can lead. If a report just landed and you need readers, the report can lead. The donate path stays available without crowding the others off the first screen.

Label the paths with verbs a person can picture. Give, apply, volunteer, read the program, refer a family. "Get involved" and "learn more" postpone the meaning. A visitor under time pressure will not click a verb that hides the destination. They will leave, or they will click donate because it was the only clear noun, even when they were trying to join.

Each path should say what happens next, in a clause. Apply, and a coordinator replies within the window you keep. Give, and you receive a receipt and a note about what the fund covers. Read, and you get the current program description, not a campaign from two years ago. The clause is the difference between a button and an invitation.

If you have only one real path this month, show one real path. A row of equal buttons that lead to stub pages is how a small team looks disorganized. Build the page around the action you can honor. Add the others when the behind-the-scenes response exists.

## Proof that it happened

One proof is enough on the homepage. A program year with a constraint, a decision, and the work in the world. The clinic added a Wednesday night because Tuesday was turning people away. The crew changed the route after a washout and still cleared the agreed miles. The constraint and the decision are what make it a proof. A single large number with no story is a billboard.

Use numbers you can point to in a report, a board packet, or a public filing. People served, nights open, miles kept, funds spent on the program versus overhead, if you are ready to say it plainly. If you cannot explain the definition, do not print the number. "Lives touched" with no method is a sad photograph made of type. Leave it off until the method is something a skeptical donor can read.

A participant's words belong here only with consent, context, and a reason. What changed for them, in their phrasing, tied to the program. No last names if that was the agreement. No details that expose someone who came for help. If you do not have consent, do not invent a composite quote. The absence is more trustworthy than a voice you wrote yourself.

Logos of funders and partners help when they are true and current. A wall of old grants implies a scale you may not have. Show the ones that shape this year's work, and link the report. A donor who needs to believe you are real will use the report as the second page. Make that handoff obvious.

## The first ten seconds

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave within 10–20 seconds unless the page has already shown a clear value. For this homepage, the value is the work and the way in. A manifesto, a slideshow of unrelated causes, and a modal asking for email all spend that window on the organization instead of the program.

Put the scene and the primary verb above the rest. The annual gala, the founder's letter, and the news module can sit lower, and only if they are current. A homepage that leads with an event from last spring tells a visitor the site is a scrapbook. Update it or remove it. Silence is cleaner than stale urgency.

The title in the browser can say the organization and the program in plain language. The visible heading can be the scene. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for a descriptive, concise title and a clear main heading. Use the heading for the human sentence. Use the title so a search result tells a stranger what you actually do. Several slogans fighting at the top will lose that clarity.

Keep the writing short enough to finish. The same research notes that people read only about a quarter of the text on pages they visit. A long essay on the homepage will hide the Wednesday clinic under the fold of good intentions. Say the scene, say who it is for, say how to enter. Link the deeper pages for the reader who stays.

## Money, without making the homepage a ledger

Donors will look for a hint that money reaches the work. You can give that hint without turning the first screen into a spreadsheet. One sentence, tied to the program: what a typical gift supports, or where to read the latest numbers. Link the report or the pricing and giving page. Do not invent a cost-per-outcome because it sounds satisfying. If you do not have a defensible figure, say what the program costs to run in the terms you do have, or send them to the report.

Participants should not have to climb over a fundraising appeal to find the service. If both audiences share the homepage, the work comes first, and giving is a clear path beside joining and reading. A visitor in need who is met with a gala video has been given an answer about whose site this is. Change the order.

Say if the program is free to participants, or what it costs, in one line. Surprising someone with a fee after they have asked for help is a trust failure. Surprising a donor by implying a service is free when it is billed is the same failure in the other direction. The homepage can say the truth in a clause and let the dedicated page explain the shape.

## Photographs and consent

Direct photography toward the work. Hands on the task, the place, the materials, the gathering, with consent you would be willing to show a board. Decline photos that use distress as the hook. A person in crisis is not a creative asset. If the work is sensitive, photograph the place, the tools, and the staff who have agreed, and let the writing carry the stakes.

Ballarat Box Sports, a public Hanabi project, is a community sports brand, not a charity appeal. The useful parallel is tone. The site shows the community doing the thing, with enough specificity that a stranger understands the world. This page can hold that same respect. The program, the place, the people as agents. The camera is a guest.

Alt text should describe the scene. "Community" and "impact" describe nothing. "Volunteers packing produce boxes in the school gym" describes the frame. Captions can add the day and the program. A caption that begs is doing the sad-photograph job in a smaller font. State the fact.

## What to bring to the build

Bring the program sentence, the primary path you can staff, one proof you can defend, and the pictures you have permission to use. If enrollment and donations are both real, bring the response window for each. The page cannot promise a coordinator who does not exist. If the report is the proof, bring the file. A homepage that links to a missing PDF is a small crack in a trust product.

Hanabi designs and builds this kind of page so the work stays in front. The stack can stay quiet. What you should feel is a fast first screen, words you can edit when the season changes, and a portal afterward for logos, consent notes, and the current report. The site is a public promise. The files behind it should be findable when the person who launched it is on leave.

Look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) when you want that homepage made with the same care as the program. Bring the sentence you would say at an intake desk. If it cannot fit on the first screen, the first screen is still about the organization, and the visitor will feel it.

Someone who accepts the work will ask what it costs to take part, or what a gift actually does. [A pricing page for a nonprofit](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-nonprofit) is the next piece, because the shape of a fee, a membership, or a gift should be visible before anyone has to write you to ask.
